E0556.summary: For Atwood, faith is a real ideal conception that leads experimental inquiry and grows into knowledge, not blind credulity; it is a common witness inferring a reality beyond experience, to be directed by reason.
E0556.body:
Atwood insists that “The faith we invite is no blind credulity” [III.3 ¶64]. Faith is a real ideal conception, however small, that leads experimental inquiry and grows into knowledge and practical experience. It is a liberty of thought that bears its own evidence. She equates it with the ideal conception: “without faith, without the ideal conception, nothing is or can be proven” [III.3 ¶64].

Later she presents faith as a witness common to all: “we have a witness which believes and infers, a reality beyond present experience” [IV.4 ¶15]. It draws the other faculties after it: “faith is the very attracting loadstone which hope pursues” [IV.4 ¶19], drawing hope, desire and reason. Faith must nevertheless be directed by reason [IV.4 ¶15–19].

E0557.summary: In the Table Talk, Atwood treats the Fall as Nature's being taken from the primal source into a will, a fall that was spiritual before it was sensible.
E0557.body: Both records come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood writes: “Nature has taken from the primal source into a will is the history of the Fall.” [APP ¶48]. The sentence is garbled as printed; apparently the Fall is Nature's being taken from the primal source into a will. She also holds that “the Fall was not at first sensible, but spiritual; the principle of the Fall is a long way back behind its effects” [APP ¶121]. Birth into this life is a continuous image of it [APP ¶121]. See also *feminine principle*, which she calls the cause of the Fall [APP ¶98].

E0558.summary: What remains of sense impressions even in trance, which must be destroyed before the understanding spirit can receive Divinity.
E0558.body: Atwood (II.2) describes the remnant of sense impressions that persists even in trance as “a false imagination, which it is requisite to destroy” [II.2 ¶10]. It must be destroyed before the understanding spirit can receive Divinity [II.2 ¶10].

E0559.summary: An address at the Faraday Society's opening meeting, cited by Atwood as an example of the modern view of alchemists as deluded crucible-brooders, which she criticizes.
E0559.body: Atwood cites this address as a sample of the modern view that the alchemists were deluded crucible-brooders, and she criticizes it [I.1 ¶33]. The passage she quotes derives a word from an alchemist's obscure style: “from whose peculiar and mysterious style of writing we derive the word geber or gibberish” [I.1 ¶33].

E0561.summary: In the Table Talk, the feminine principle is that which is above, drawing the self-willed source upward by love; it is the cause of the Fall and, advanced, of restoration.
E0561.body: Both points come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood identifies the feminine principle with Wisdom and the heart life: “that which is above (the feminine principle, --- Wisdom, --- the heart life)” [APP ¶98]. It draws the self-willed source upward by love, and the self-willed source thereby becomes a passive feminine principle [APP ¶98]. It works both ways: “As the feminine spirit is the cause of the Fall”, so, advanced, it is the cause of restoration [APP ¶98].

E0562.summary: The active agent by which one life works on another (or a thing on itself), opening and dissolving it so that a higher life is freed and exalted; Hermes calls it the Key of the philosophers.
E0562.body:
**Atwood's usage.** A ferment is a superior power that frees the subject-matter: “being set free by the force of a superior ferment or attraction” [I.2 ¶4]. The Ether is called fermenting, and “the fermented Spirit assimilates the Light throughout” [I.2 ¶8]. It is a thing's own agent of change and converts it into another nature with nothing foreign added. In the Art the Spirit is raised “by its won prepared must or leaven” and gains virtue “in proportion to the virtue which it has acquired in the fermentation” [I.2 ¶48]. The Stone is exalted by fermentation within its own kind, and “every ferment begets its own exaltation” [I.3 n55]. Reason acts as a ferment and “would gather all up, as a ferment” into its Light [III.1 ¶21]. She contrasts “that body which is gold (not a brazen ferment)” [III.1 ¶19]. Sulfur is called the golden ferment, and the rising light keeps “a fermental odor of the body” so that the soul does not depart altogether [III.1 ¶53]. The result depends on the agent: “according to the virtue of the fermenting principle is the result obtained”. The philosophic matter “is purified by successive interchanging of ferments”, as sap becomes wine [IV.1 ¶44, ¶46].

**Hermes** compares the ferment to leaven in dough: “see how the ferment in this case doth change the former natures to another thing” [I.3 ¶58]. It must be kindred, since “there is no ferment otherwise than from a kindred nature” [I.3 ¶58]. It whitens, prevents combustion, holds the tincture and joins bodies, and it is the Key of the philosophers [I.3 ¶58].

**Other voices.** In a note whose voice is unclear, “the inquisitive light once entering as a ferment” meets its proper pole and converts the medium into itself [II.3 n40]. *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon* requires that “Which Ferment must be of such a thing, As was the workes begyning;” [III.1 ¶65]. In the poem this means Luna for the white and Sol for the red, each worked alone with the Lion's blood. It is added warm to the Magnet as a fourth part, and continual fermentation multiplies the Medicine [III.1 ¶65]. Atwood's “Rational Ferment” [III.1 ¶66] is a separate term.

**Table Talk (APP, later layer).** Here a ferment is the action of one life on another: “When one life being fermented throws its life to another equally fermented” [APP ¶42]. Seven is “a Rest from the ferment or action of the Vitalizing or Divine principles” [APP ¶69]. The reader is told to “so ferment the whole including spirit of your life that it, the former, opens, corrupts, dissolves” [APP ¶126], and “each fermented spirit advances upon its origin” [APP ¶111]. *Fermented* = elaborated: “perfectly elaborated --- i.e., fermented”, said of the individual Logos that transmutes the whole being [APP ¶101].

E0563.summary: In a passage quoted from Aristhenes, that into which the 'least' thing is to be drawn by artifice; the text does not define it.
E0563.body: Atwood quotes Aristhenes, who says to “draw it by artifice into the true ferment of philosophers” [II.2 ¶26]. The thing to be drawn in is the ‘least’ thing. The passage does not define the term further. See *ferment*.

E0564.summary: The core operation in which a life worked by a kindred life dissolves and passes into a higher state; Atwood's best image of the Divine Art and the final cementing of the Stone's union.
E0564.body:
**Main text (Atwood).** Fermentation is the subject's artificial progress to perfection: “In its artificial fermentation and progress towards perfection” [I.2 ¶37]. Liquid analogies denote “the fermental principle of the spirit and her distilled quintessence” [I.2 ¶33]. The chapter title names “the spontaneous fermentation which the Vital Spirit undergoes, and the change that is thereby effected in the Passive Subject” [III.1 ¶9]. Modern practice does not push this process to the uttermost [III.1 ¶9]. Atwood distinguishes two kinds: “there is a twofold fermentation --- a spiritual and a bodily” [IV.3 ¶21]. The spiritual kind multiplies the tinctures, and the bodily kind incorporates the medicine into gold or silver. Fermentation is the last operation, in which the Stone's union is finally cemented and its parts agree and relate to the external world: “which union or consummation of its transmutative virtue is called Fermentation” [IV.3 ¶27]. She asserts an identity with the Kabalah: “that which in the Kabalah is denominated the union of man, reduced to the simplicity of the Monad, with God, that in metaphysico-chemistry is called Fermentation” [IV.3 ¶27]. The Stone is fermented with its own metal (silver for the White, gold for the Red), which Atwood reads as Light [IV.3 ¶27].

**Eudoxus.** His Fifth Key operation is “the Fermentation of the Stone with the perfect body” [IV.3 ¶14]. The Stone is joined, as leaven and through the Spirit, with the Perfect Body, so that the whole becomes a leaven able to multiply.

**Table Talk (APP, later layer).** Here fermentation is the core operation: a life fermented by its similar passes into a further state, and this is repeated over and over. “The word fermentation conveys an idea of the perfecting principle and of the possibility of transmutation beyond any other word”, and “it is the best image of the Divine Art which earthly processes give” [APP ¶27]. One life is worked by another so that both dissolve and are reproduced in a third. Unlike ordinary generation, the result is exalted: “spiritual generation is according to the fermentative law”, an ascending process [APP ¶132].

E0565.summary: The power of vital melioration that man possesses whole within himself, for the rectification of Nature's Law.
E0565.body: Atwood holds that man has within himself “the whole fermentative virtue, motive, and principle of vital melioration” for the rectification of Nature's Law [IV.4 ¶3].

E0566.summary: Proverbial sayings cited in the Table Talk in support of avoiding haste and excess in the work, higher or lower.
E0566.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood cites “Festina lente, Ne quid nimis” in support of avoiding haste and excess in the work, whether higher or lower [APP ¶110].

E0567.summary: A philosopher named with Kant and Schelling, whose metaphysics Atwood criticizes as falling short of objective realization; in the Table Talk he saw the Absolute ground without experiencing it.
E0567.body: In the main text Atwood groups Kant, Fichte and Schelling and criticizes their metaphysics. It ends in void non-entity and skepticism and falls short of objective realization, though she ranks Schelling above the other two [III.2 ¶31]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she says Fichte broke through into the Absolute ground, seeing it but without experiencing it [APP ¶96]. He appears again in the same list as one who ‘knew it’ [APP ¶117].

E0568.summary: Translator of Plato and of the works imputed to Hermes, whose Latin version of the Asclepian Dialogues and Poimander Atwood cites; he explained the art theoretically.
E0568.body: Atwood cites Ficinus's Latin version of the Asclepian Dialogues and the Poimander [I.1 ¶7, I.1 n11]. She calls him the translator of Plato and of the works imputed to Hermes. He explained the art theoretically, and she cites his *Liber de Arte Chemica* (Marsilii Ficini Florent.) [I.1 ¶64, I.1 n68]. He also appears as “Ficinus the Platonist” in a list [I.1 ¶39].

E0569.summary: In a quoted monk's continuation of Basil Valentine, something instituted by one who has befriended Vulcan; the text does not explain it.
E0569.body: The monk who continues Basil Valentine says that only one who has “firmly contracted friendship with Vulcan, and instituted the Fiery bath of Love” can demonstrate the separation of venom from the Medicine [IV.1 ¶40]. The expression is not explained.

E0570.summary: In a recipe quoted from Eirenaeus, an ingredient (four parts) bearing the Magic Steel in its belly, joined to nine parts Lodestone; the text does not explain it.
E0570.body: Atwood quotes Eirenaeus: “Take four parts of our Fiery Dragon, which bears in his belly the Magic Steel” [IV.1 ¶43]. The Fiery Dragon is to be conjoined to nine parts Lodestone [IV.1 ¶43]. The passage does not explain it.

E0571.summary: In Eudoxus, what animates the Water once the faeces are washed free of blackness; it works all the wonders of the Art.
E0571.body: Eudoxus says that once the faeces are washed free of blackness, “your Water shall be animated with this Fiery Essence, which works all the wonders of our Art” [IV.3 ¶8].

E0572.summary: The trial that reason is artificially constrained not to escape.
E0572.body: Atwood speaks of reason “being artificially constrained, lest it should escape the fiery ordeal” [I.3 n50].

E0573.summary: What the two warring dragons become when decocted in their own venom; for Atwood, a state beyond the four degrees, neuter from all yet partaking of all.
E0573.body: A French adept quoted by Atwood says the two warring dragons, “being decocted totally in their own venom, are turned into a Fifth Essence” [III.1 ¶58]. Atwood describes it as made beyond the four precedent degrees of perfection: “neuter from all, yet partaking of all in perpetuity of union” [III.3 ¶32]. It is embodied but not subject to gross corporeity [III.3 ¶32].

E0574.summary: The end or purpose into whose supernatural fixity Art brings the Matter; hidden in ordinary life but manifest in Alchemy.
E0574.body:
For Atwood, the Matter's alterations end when it “is brought by Art into the supernatural fixity of its Final Cause” [III.2 ¶22]. Final causes are ends or purposes. They are hidden in ordinary life, but in Alchemy, in act as in effect, “Final Causes are of all things most manifestly revealed” [III.4 ¶9]. The superior power filling the soul is “proximate to the Final Cause” [III.4 ¶6].

In IV.2 a passage of the Master carries a gloss whose voice is unclear: “the boundary of hearts (i.e., the Final Cause)” [IV.2 ¶14]. It enters above the Foliated Sulphur when fire is poured on it. Compare the generated Being, “perceiving itself indeed to be the Final Object of its own First Cause, is good” [IV.2 ¶8]. See also *First Cause*.

E0575.summary: The secret, vital fire of the philosophers, distinct from common fire; variously identified with Intellect, the life of man, the essence of life, the sulfur and seed of gold.
E0575.body:
**Atwood.** “Our fire” is the philosophers' own fire, “magical, creative, vital” [I.3 n41]. It is most subtle and extremely volatile, and it vivifies, depurates and segregates; it is distinct from common fire. “Some call it the miracle of the world” [I.3 n41]. The True matter is discovered by “no other Fire but that of Intellect” [III.2 ¶62], sublimed and fortified in its efficient source. She takes “the life of man therein circulating to be a pure fire” [IV.4 ¶4], incorporated in an ethereal vapour and containing the Universal Efficient. The method of ascent is “that artistic fabrication of the Fire which Prometheus received from Vulcan” [IV.4 ¶8]. In the Table Talk (APP, later layer) fire is the medium through which the Divine Will conducts Light: “the fire here is our chaotic will in potentiality”, and “it is the basis of our microcosmic recreation” [APP ¶97].

**Quoted authorities.** For the scholiast, “the essence of life, says the scholiast, is nothing else than a pure, naked, unmingled Fire” [I.3 n22]. It is celestial and generating, not elementary, and it is “the temperate unguent, which is fire” [I.3 ¶24]. Sendivogius says: “Fire, says the adept philosopher, is the purest and most worthy of all the elements” [II.4 ¶39]. “It is also in all things indiscernibly.” [II.4 ¶39], moved only by God's will. It bears God's seal and is the death and separation of everything compounded. Eirenaeus urges: “be not so careful of the fire of the Athanor as of your internal Fire” [III.1 ¶14]. He identifies it: “Our fire is the true sulfur of Gold, says Eirenaeus”, and “this is the seed of gold, involved in many links, and held prisoner, as it were, in a deep dungeon” [III.1 ¶14]. This fire is imprisoned in the hard, dry body and freed by our water, and it appears in the Third Menstrual [III.1 ¶14]. Atwood names Eirenaeus' ‘internal fire of the sulfur of thy water’ as the vital perscrutinator [III.1 ¶13]. Pontanus says: “seek to know this Fire with all thy soul, that so thou mayest attain to thy desire; for it is the key of all the philosophers” [III.1 ¶37]. Vaughan writes that “the excitation of the Fire is a very trivial, slight, almost a ridiculous thing”, yet it holds all the secrets of corruption and generation [III.4 ¶38]. An Adept names “the natural, unnatural, and the supernatural Fires”, which must be lit quickly so that none puts out another; a Fourth supervenes over them [IV.2 ¶11]. Sendivogius also says to “put them into Our Fire and let there be made of them a dry liquor” [IV.3 ¶21]. See also *Fire of the Wise*.

E0576.summary: In the Paracelsian passage Atwood quotes, the life-fire in man, called Antimony by adepts, which does nothing excellent while immured but flows forth as panacea after purgation.
E0576.body: In a Paracelsian passage the fire of life is the life-fire in man: “our fire of life (called Antimony by adepts, can effect nothing comparatively excellent whilst it is immured” [III.1 ¶10]. Like unlit fuel, it does nothing while immured. After purgation the pure life flows forth as panacea [III.1 ¶10]. The same passage asserts the identity with Antimony.

E0577.summary: A fire named in several contexts: what drew the Magians toward nature's central source, what besieges the bound serpents, and that by which the Matter brings forth Orus; it is not defined.
E0577.body: Atwood says the Magians were “drawn about the fire of nature, as it were, into communication with her central source” [I.1 ¶39]. Cornelius Agrippa's disciple advises: “Thou must incamp against them with the fire of nature”, meaning against the bound serpents [III.1 ¶50]. The text does not say whether this is the ‘fire of the natural life’ of III.1 ¶43. The Matter brings forth Orus “by the Fire of nature lawfully conceived” [III.3 ¶62]. None of these passages explains the term.

E0578.summary: In Sendivogius, the fire of the second operation, different from that of the first.
E0578.body: Sendivogius directs the work to be set on “the fire of putrefaction and generation, not on such a one as thou didst in the first operation” [IV.3 ¶21].

E0579.summary: In Eudoxus, the secret fire that is the only instrument of sublimation, dissolving the Stone gently into Water; no philosopher has openly revealed it.
E0579.body: Eudoxus calls it “the Fire of the Wise, which is the only instrument which can work this sublimation” [IV.3 ¶5]. It dissolves the Stone naturally and without violence into Water. It is the Secret Fire: “No philosopher has ever openly revealed this Secret Fire” [IV.3 ¶5]. It is also called “this Secret Fire, and this powerful agent, which works all the wonders of the Art” [IV.3 ¶5]. It is known by its described characters and by divine gift. Eudoxus also says “the whole compound, is made perfect by the action of our Fire” [IV.3 ¶7], but he does not assert that this is the Fire of the Wise.

E0580.summary: In a quoted adept, a spirit rooted in the spiritual fire earth, from which it is fed by a secret influx.
E0580.body: The adept Atwood quotes says the Fire Spirit is rooted in the spiritual fire earth and “receives from it a secret influx upon which it feeds” [II.3 ¶41].

E0581.summary: The region consciousness enters after the middle region (Atwood) or after the Aquaster (a quoted adept), where invisible things are seen; the text does not define it further.
E0581.body: Atwood says that after the middle region, at the dark descent, consciousness “enters the Fire World” [II.3 ¶16]. The adept she quotes places it after the Aquaster: one who has “entered the Fire World, sees what is both invisible and incredible to common men” [II.3 ¶41]. Neither passage defines it further.

E0582.summary: Cited in the Table Talk, where Atwood reads graven images as the practical result of self-centering and stopping in finite gifts as idolatry.
E0582.body: Both citations come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood interprets graven images (the Second Commandment) as the practical result of self-centering, which violates the First [APP ¶100]. She also cites the commandments for the view that stopping in finite gifts is idolatry [APP ¶135].

E0583.summary: The cause of a being's existence, which each has in himself; the top of the ascending series of causes, into which Reason re-enters and the only proper object of seeking.
E0583.body:
Atwood places the First Cause at the top of the ascending series of causes, the ‘Final Cause of all’. The lowest effect reverses it: “the last and lowest effect, in which all the attributes of the First Cause are not only deficient but reversed” [III.2 ¶54]. Selfhood is raised into it. In a passage whose voice is unclear, expulsive life draws consciousness away from it: “drawn without to a debilitated consciousness away from its First Cause” [II.1 ¶21]. In IV.2 it is essence, the subsisting as a particular thing. “cause and principle form the First Why” [IV.2 ¶7]. “the speculative Motive of the first Cause is finally produced in reversionary order from the Third” and passes by the Second into the Fourth [IV.2 ¶8]. It is the only proper object of seeking. The aim is to “attain to that supremacy of Reason which re-enters to its First Cause” [IV.2 ¶18], and “the consummating knowledge of the First Cause” comes in quietude and cessation of mental energy [IV.2 ¶33]. At the end of the work “the Ethereal Hypostasis revolves in its First Cause” [IV.3 ¶62], and the upright Mind of Man “co-operates with the First Cause” [IV.4 ¶32].

Aristotle, quoted on deliberation, uses the phrase differently: men work back from the proposed end through its media “until they arrive at the first Cause which is discovered in the last place” [IV.1 ¶30].

In the Table Talk (APP, later layer) each being has the cause of its existence in himself. Since Existence is one, knowing it is knowing the cause of all: “the consciousness can be brought into contact with its First Cause” [APP ¶6]. See also *Final Cause*.

E0584.summary: What the dissolving water reduces all metals into, glossed as water.
E0584.body: Atwood says the dissolving water “reduces them into their first ens, or water”, speaking of all metals [I.3 n12]. The first ens is thus identified with water.

E0585.summary: An initial step whose knowledge, together with volatilizing the fixed tincture, admits one to the temple of Divine Science; the text does not explain it.
E0585.body: Atwood writes: “He who knows the first entrance” and how to volatilize the fixed tincture is admitted to the temple of Divine Science [IV.4 ¶32]. The text does not explain what the first entrance is.

E0586.summary: In Norton's verse, the foundational knowledge required of anyone who hopes 'to come by Lakimie'.
E0586.body: Norton, quoted by Atwood, requires of anyone hoping ‘to come by Lakimie’: “He must know hys first filosophie,” [IV.2 ¶5].
